title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
subtitle: How web transport evolved from text-based serial connections to binary TCP multiplexing and finally QUIC over UDP.
keyTakeaways: HTTP/1.1 suffers from Application-Layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking, forcing browsers to open up to 6 parallel TCP connections per domain.
HTTP/2 introduces binary framing, HPACK header compression, and stream multiplexing over a single TCP connection: but remains vulnerable to TCP-Layer HoL blocking on packet loss.
HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP, multiplexing independent streams in user space so a lost packet only stalls the single affected stream, while enabling 0-RTT/1-RTT combined TLS handshakes.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: In HTTP/1.1, requests on a persistent connection must be processed strictly in order: if Request #1 takes 200ms on the server, Request #2 behind it cannot receive its response first (Application-Layer Head-of-Line blocking). Browsers worked around this by opening 6 parallel TCP connections per origin and using hacks like CSS sprites and domain sharding. **HTTP/2** solved this at the application layer by breaking every request and response into small binary frames tagged with a `Stream ID`, allowing hundreds of concurrent requests to interleave over a **single TCP connection**, alongside HPACK header compression.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: HTTP/1.1 suffers from Application-Layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking, forcing browsers to open up to 6 parallel TCP connections per domain.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: HTTP/2 introduces binary framing, HPACK header compression, and stream multiplexing over a single TCP connection: but remains vulnerable to TCP-Layer HoL blocking on packet loss.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3:
bullets: **HTTP/2 over TCP**: Provides universal support across all load balancers, corporate firewalls, and runtimes; low cpu overhead due to kernel tcp offload (tso); required transport for grpc. Best suited for Internal data-center microservice communication (gRPC), stable broadband connections, and standard cloud backends.

**HTTP/3 over QUIC (UDP)**: Provides zero cross-stream hol blocking on lossy mobile networks, 1-rtt/0-rtt handshakes, seamless wi-fi-to-cellular connection migration. Best suited for Mobile apps on spotty cellular connections, global CDN edge delivery (Cloudflare/Fastly), and latency-critical web apps.
Binary Framing Layer: Parses compact binary frames instead of error-prone newline-delimited ASCII text.
HPACK Header Compression: Eliminates redundant transmission of bloated `Cookie` and `User-Agent` headers across requests.
Combined Transport + Crypto Handshake: QUIC embeds TLS 1.3 directly into its handshake, requiring only 1 RTT for new connections and 0-RTT for resumed connections.

Connection Migration (Connection ID): When a user walks out of their house and switches from Wi-Fi IP to 5G Cellular IP, TCP connections break. QUIC identifies connections by a 64-bit `Connection ID`, surviving IP/port changes seamlessly!

codeSnippet.title: Comparing Handshake Round-Trips Across HTTP Generations
codeSnippet.code:
/*
 * Connection Setup Latency before First Byte of Application Request Sent:
 *
 * 1. HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2 over TLS 1.2:
 *    - TCP 3-Way Handshake:        1 RTT
 *    - TLS 1.2 Handshake:          2 RTTs
 *    - Total Setup Cost:           3 RTTs before HTTP request!
 *
 * 2. HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3:
 *    - TCP 3-Way Handshake:        1 RTT
 *    - TLS 1.3 Handshake:          1 RTT
 *    - Total Setup Cost:           2 RTTs
 *
 * 3. HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP with built-in TLS 1.3):
 *    - Transport + TLS Combined:   1 RTT (New connection)
 *    - Session Resumption:         0 RTT (Send HTTP request in very first packet!)
 */

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Internal data-center microservice communication (gRPC), stable broadband connections, and standard cloud backends, suited for environments requiring Universal support across all load balancers, corporate firewalls, and runtimes; low CPU overhead due to kernel TCP offload (TSO); required transport for gRPC.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Mobile apps on spotty cellular connections, global CDN edge delivery (Cloudflare/Fastly), and latency-critical web apps, where Zero cross-stream HoL blocking on lossy mobile networks, 1-RTT/0-RTT handshakes, seamless Wi-Fi-to-Cellular connection migration.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: To eliminate TCP-level Head-of-Line blocking without waiting 15 years for every OS kernel and middlebox router on Earth to upgrade TCP, Google designed **QUIC** (standardized as the transport layer for **HTTP/3**). Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: suffers from tcp-layer head-of-line blocking on lossy networks (>1-2% packet loss); breaks when client ip changes (wi-fi to 5g).

**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: higher cpu usage in user-space udp encryption/packet pacing, some enterprise networks block udp port 443 (requires fallback to http/2).
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP, multiplexing independent streams in user space so a lost packet only stalls the single affected stream, while enabling 0-RTT/1-RTT combined TLS handshakes.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: If your system design involves mobile clients on flaky networks (e.g., Uber driver app, WhatsApp, Instagram), explicitly recommend HTTP/3 (QUIC) at the CDN edge for connection migration (switching from Wi-Fi to 5G without dropping in-flight uploads) and 0-RTT resumption.

tradeOffs.cons: Suffers from TCP-layer Head-of-Line blocking on lossy networks (>1-2% packet loss); breaks when client IP changes (Wi-Fi to 5G).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal data-center microservice communication (gRPC), stable broadband connections, and standard cloud backends.

tradeOffs.cons: Higher CPU usage in user-space UDP encryption/packet pacing, some enterprise networks block UDP port 443 (requires fallback to HTTP/2).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Mobile apps on spotty cellular connections, global CDN edge delivery (Cloudflare/Fastly), and latency-critical web apps.
